questions.question: One die is rolled. What is P(3 or 5)?
questions.explanation: A single roll can't be both 3 and 5, so the events are mutually exclusive: 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.question: A fair coin is flipped twice. What is P(heads both times)?
questions.explanation: The flips are independent, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.question: One card is drawn from a standard deck. What is P(heart or king)?
questions.explanation: 13 hearts + 4 kings − 1 king of hearts (counted twice) = 16 cards, so 16/52 = 4/13.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is P(both are aces)?
questions.explanation: 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221. The second draw has only 3 aces left among 51 cards. Using 4/52 × 4/52 = 1/169 wrongly treats the draws as independent.

questions.question: A die is rolled 4 times. What is P(at least one 6)?
questions.explanation: Use the complement: P(no 6 in four rolls) = (5/6)^4 ≈ 0.4823, so P(at least one 6) ≈ 0.5177.

questions.question: A and B are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.explanation: If A happens, B cannot, so knowing A changes the probability of B to 0. That is dependence. Mutually exclusive and independent are nearly opposites.
